content: Lead poisoning continues to be one of the most prevalent and preventable environmental health issues affecting children, despite significant progress in the United States in reducing the number of children with elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). One of the objectives of the Healthy People 2010 initiative is to eliminate BLLs greater than 10 µg/dL among children nationwide. Children in the U.S. who live in poorly maintained housing built before 1978 are at the highest risk for elevated BLLs due to frequent exposure to lead-based paint, lead-contaminated house dust, and soil. The prevalence of elevated BLLs among U.S. children is approximately 2%. In New Hampshire, blood lead screening is mandated for newly arrived refugee children aged 6 months to 16 years. Starting in May 2004, 242 refugee children, primarily from Africa, were resettled in New Hampshire. Of these, 96 children underwent two rounds of BLL testing. The first blood samples were collected within 90 days of their arrival, and the second samples were collected 3 to 6 months after resettlement. Most of the children initially had capillary BLLs below 10 µg/dL, but 5 children, who were siblings of cases, had BLLs ranging from 11 to 73 µg/dL. Eleven families had at least one child with a BLL greater than 20 µg/dL. Environmental investigations revealed moderate lead hazards in the children’s residences and lead-contaminated soil in play areas. Additionally, children with elevated BLLs exhibited signs of severe chronic malnutrition. Approximately 2% of the children had severe growth retardation, defined as a height-for-age Z-score below -2 (approximately the 2nd percentile on standard pediatric growth curves). Among the 40 children for whom weight was measured, 10 (25%) showed evidence of failure to gain weight or weight loss, with weight-for-height Z-scores below -2 (approximately the 2nd percentile). Recommendations: Primary prevention of elevated BLLs should ideally involve ensuring that all children live in lead-safe housing, particularly those with poor nutritional status and limited awareness of lead poisoning risks. However, to reduce the risk of lead exposure in refugee children, the following measures are recommended: 1. Repeat BLL testing for all refugee children aged 6 months to 6 years, 3 to 6 months after they are placed in permanent residences. Older children should also be tested if warranted, regardless of initial test results. 2. Children who exhibit pica behavior (mouthing or eating non-food items), especially soil, are at risk for lead poisoning regardless of the age of their housing. This behavior is common in certain refugee populations and warrants close monitoring. The New Hampshire case study highlights that while some children had elevated BLLs upon arrival in the U.S., the majority did not. Follow-up screening conducted 60 to 90 days after placement in permanent residences revealed elevated BLLs ranging from 11 to 72 µg/dL. Refugee children are typically eligible for Medicaid, WIC, and other social services for at least 8 months after resettlement, regardless of their family’s financial status. These services provide critical support for addressing health and nutritional needs during this vulnerable period.
